title: A toy landscape and a solver grid ask: does the search find the best valley or only the nearest one?
summary: The same two-parameter problem is drawn as three surfaces, each defined by a different objective, with the starting point, the true optimum and the path a search took. The comparison is about shape: a single smooth bowl is easy for any optimizer, a surface with many valleys is not, and a smoothed starting surface can lead the search into the right valley before the final objective is applied.

media.alt: Three columns of the same two-parameter problem, each a 3D surface above a contour map. Left: the classical WMRE objective, one smooth bowl. Middle: a fixed exponent p = 0.05, a rugged surface with many grey local-minimum dots. Right: an annealed exponent from 4 to 0.05, the same rugged surface with dashed contours for the smoother starting surface. A black start dot, a green star for the true optimum and a red search path are drawn.

A toy 2D search landscape shown three ways: classical WMRE's objective surface, a fixed-p power-mean surface, and the annealed-p surface a genetic-algorithm search actually sees as p anneals from 4 to 0.05 during the run — the annealing is what smooths a rugg

read_the_figure.question: Does the shape of the objective surface decide whether a search from a given starting point finds the true optimum?
read_the_figure.axes: Axes z1 and z2 are the two parameters (standardized, from minus 1 to 1 in the contour panels). Height and colour are the objective value of that column's objective, with its own colour bar. Top row: the surface in 3D. Bottom row: the same surface as filled contours from above. Column titles: the classical WMRE objective, a fixed-exponent power-mean objective (p = 0.05), and an annealed one (p going from 4 to 0.05, normalized). Black dot: start. Green star: true optimum, known here because the problem is constructed. Red line: the search path. Small grey dots: local minima. Dashed light contours in the right column: the pre-anneal surface at the starting exponent.
look_at: Left column first: one smooth bowl with its minimum at the green star. Any reasonable optimizer slides down it. Note the objective values reach several thousand.

Middle column: the same optimum is now surrounded by many grey dots. Each dot is a valley a downhill search can stop in. Note the colour bar: values only reach about two and a half, so the columns are not on the same scale.
Right column: the filled contours are the final surface; the dashed contours show the smoother surface the search starts on. Follow the red path: does it cross several valleys before settling?
Always compare where the red path ends with the position of the green star, not with the nearest valley bottom.
In the contour panels, check how far the start (black dot) is from the star, and whether the path in the middle column stops early in a valley on the way.

The companion grid figure puts three optimizers (gradient descent, GA, CMA-ES) against the three objectives, with two printed numbers in each panel: obj and dist. Compare dist across the grid (it is the distance to the true optimum, the same in every panel) and never obj, because the objective changes from row to row.
read_the_figure.proves: The figure shows what a surface looks like and what one search did on it. It proves that the rugged surface has many local minima and that the paths differ between columns. It does not prove that one objective is better in general: the surface is a constructed toy problem, and one start point and one solver is one sample.
if_wrong: A path that ends at a grey dot far from the green star: the search stopped in a local minimum. The objective value there can look good while the parameters are wrong.
A path that jitters in a small cluster near the end: a stochastic search at its resolution limit, or a surface so flat that steps are noise.
A start point very close to the true optimum: any method will look good. The figure that starts from a poor guess is the harder test.
Columns drawn with different colour bars read as if equal: the same colour does not mean the same value across columns.
In the grid, a panel with a small obj but a dist near 0.6 is a local minimum; the same solver giving identical numbers under two objectives is stuck in the same valley.
must_check: Each column has its own colour bar and axis range, stated.
The true optimum is marked and the problem is synthetic, so its location is known.
Start point and solver for the drawn path are given (the optimizer-grid figure of the project names them).
Local minima are marked so the reader can count the traps.
The path is plotted in the same coordinates as the contours (here z1, z2 in the standardized range).

terms.meaning: The value that the optimizer minimizes, drawn as a function of the parameters. Its shape sets how hard the search is.
A point lower than all its neighbours but not the lowest overall. A downhill search that starts in its basin stops there.
The lowest point of the whole surface. In this toy problem it is known by construction and drawn as a green star.
Starting on an easy, smooth version of the objective and gradually changing it into the final one, tracking the minimum as it moves.
For positive numbers s_1..s_D, the generalized mean of exponent p. It is an ordinary average when p = 1, a geometric mean as p goes to 0, and it approaches the largest value as p grows.
The sequence of points an optimizer visits; for a population method it is the path of the best point.
The objective rescaled (for example to the range zero to one) so that surfaces with very different magnitudes can be drawn with comparable colours.

remember: Smooth bowl: any descent method works. Many valleys: where you start decides where you end.
A local minimum can have a respectable objective value and a wrong parameter vector.
Different columns have different scales; compare shapes, not heights.
A toy problem with a known optimum measures the method, not the data.
One path from one start is one sample, not a result.

understand.title: Why the surface changes with the exponent
understand.text: The three objectives combine the same underlying errors with different exponents. With the classical average the biggest errors dominate and the surface is a broad bowl. With a small exponent every error counts on a proportional (logarithmic) scale, which brings out many local features. The figure shows what that does to the geometry, which is why the search difficulty differs.

understand.title: What annealing buys
understand.text: Starting on a smoother surface lets the search settle into the right broad region first. As the exponent is lowered the surface is deformed continuously into the rugged final one, and the search follows the minimum it was already in. It is a standard continuation idea; the figure's dashed contours are the starting surface.

understand.title: Why a known optimum matters
understand.text: On real data the true best parameters are unknown, so one can only compare objective values. A constructed surface lets you measure the distance to the truth and so test whether a method finds the right answer, not just a low value.

steps.title: One step of gradient descent
steps.note: Move a fraction alpha of the way down the local slope. The path follows the downhill direction, so it ends at the bottom of whichever basin it started in.

steps.title: On a bowl it converges if the step is small enough
steps.note: The error shrinks by the factor one minus alpha lambda each step; it converges when that factor lies between minus one and one. A steep direction (large lambda) sets the largest usable step.

steps.title: A minimum is where the slope vanishes and the surface curves up
steps.note: Every grey dot satisfies this; so does the green star. Nothing in this condition tells them apart, which is why the surface shape matters.

steps.title: Continuation: deform a smooth surface into the final one
steps.note: A generic homotopy. At t = 0 the minimum is easy to find; at each step the previous minimum is the starting point for the next. In the figure the exponent plays the role of the schedule, and the dashed contours are the early surface.

steps.title: Rescaling to compare surfaces
steps.note: One common normalization, which maps every surface to the range zero to one. The ordering of points is unchanged, so the valleys stay where they are; only the heights are comparable.

steps.title: The power mean of a set of errors
steps.note: Standard definition. Raising to p before averaging changes how much each condition counts: a large p lets the largest errors dominate the average, a small p lets all conditions count more evenly.

steps.title: p = 1 is the ordinary average
steps.note: This is the classical mean of the errors. One condition with a very large error can supply most of the total.

steps.title: The limit p to 0 is the geometric mean
steps.note: Use e^x close to 1 + x for small p, then ln(1+x) close to x. So M_p tends to the geometric mean exp of the average log. Equal factors of improvement count equally, whichever condition they occur on.

worked.title: Largest safe step on a bowl
worked.problem: Along the steepest direction a bowl has curvature lambda = 25 (in the parameter units used). What is the largest step size alpha for which gradient descent converges, and what is the shrink factor per step at alpha = 0.05?

solution.text: The limit is two over lambda.
At alpha = 0.05 the factor per step is

worked.answer: alpha must be below 0.08; at 0.05 the error is cut to a quarter at every step.

analyze.q: The fixed-exponent surface has the same global optimum as the annealed one at the end. Why can a search on one fail while the other succeeds?
analyze.hint: Same final surface, different route to it.

analyze.q: A path ends at a grey dot with a lower objective value than the start. Has the search succeeded?
analyze.hint: Compare the distance to the green star.

analyze.q: Why are the colour bars of the columns so different?
analyze.hint: The objectives are defined differently; one is not normalized the same way.

evaluate.q: What would you need to claim that annealing is better than a fixed exponent, based on a figure like this?
evaluate.hint: Many starts, many solvers, a distance-to-optimum statistic, and more than one toy surface.

evaluate.q: Is a toy surface with a known optimum a fair test for a real kinetics problem?
evaluate.hint: It tests the optimizer logic; it does not test the realism of the data or the model.

create: Draw the same three surfaces with one shared normalized colour bar, so that the ruggedness is comparable between columns.
Design a fourth column with a still lower exponent. What would you expect to see in the surface, and what should the path look like?

checks.hint: It is known because the problem is built, not measured.
checks.answer: The true optimum of the constructed toy problem: the correct parameter vector, which is known because the problem was made from it.

checks.q: Gradient descent on f = 1/2 lambda x^2 with lambda = 10: what is the largest step size that converges?
A search path ends in a valley with low objective but far from the green star. What is it?
checks.answer: A local minimum. The stopping criterion cannot tell it from the global one; only the known optimum, or more starts, can.

checks.q: Is it fair to compare heights of the surfaces in the left and middle columns?
checks.answer: No: the left objective reaches thousands and the middle only about two and a half. Only the shapes can be compared.

checks.q: How would you test whether the conclusion depends on the starting point?
checks.answer: Run the same optimizers from a set of starts spread over the domain, including a poor corner start, and report the fraction of runs that end near the true optimum.

checks.q: In the solver grid two panels print dist 0.629 and a third in the same row prints 0.004. What do you conclude about the solvers?
checks.answer: The solver with 0.004 reached the true optimum on this surface and start; the ones with about 0.63 stopped in a local minimum. One start and one seed each: a demonstration, not a ranking.
